title: Burgundy Level 1 Comprehensive Assessment Question Bank

questions.question: Where is Burgundy located in France?
questions.explanation: Burgundy is located in eastern France, beginning about 300 km southeast of Paris. Its main cities include Dijon and Beaune.

questions.question: What climate type does Burgundy have?
questions.explanation: Burgundy has a continental climate with four distinct seasons — cold winters and warm (but not hot) summers — ideal conditions for Pinot Noir and Chardonnay.

questions.question: Which monastic order contributed most to the development of Burgundy wine?
questions.explanation: Cistercian monks carefully studied the differences between plots, pioneering the concept of 'terroir' and establishing rigorous standards for viticulture and winemaking — an enormous contribution to Burgundy's development.

questions.question: What UNESCO designation did Burgundy's "Climats" receive in 2015?
questions.explanation: In 2015, Burgundy's Climats — 1,247 precisely delineated vineyard plots — were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, recognizing their unique cultural and historical value.

questions.question: Which grape variety is primarily used for Burgundy red wine?
questions.explanation: Burgundy red wine is made almost exclusively from Pinot Noir. This single-variety tradition is one of Burgundy's defining characteristics, in sharp contrast to Bordeaux's blending tradition.

questions.question: What is Chardonnay primarily used to make in Burgundy?
questions.explanation: Chardonnay is a white grape variety used primarily for white wine in Burgundy. Burgundy is Chardonnay's homeland, and its white wines are considered the world benchmark.

questions.question: In Burgundy's four-tier classification system, which tier has the lowest yield but the highest quality?
questions.explanation: Grand Cru accounts for only 1% of Burgundy's total production and represents the highest quality tier. These vineyards enjoy the finest terroir and produce wines with the greatest aging potential.

questions.question: On a Burgundy label, if only "Chambertin" is shown without a village name, what tier is this?
questions.explanation: A Grand Cru label displays only the vineyard name, without the village name, because a Grand Cru is itself an independent AOC. A Premier Cru label instead shows "village name + 1er Cru + vineyard name."

questions.question: What does "Mis en bouteille au domaine" mean on a label?
questions.explanation: "Mis en bouteille au domaine" means the wine was bottled at the estate, usually indicating the same domaine controlled everything from grape-growing through bottling — generally a mark of better quality assurance.

questions.question: Burgundy has six main sub-regions running north to south. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
questions.explanation: Pauillac is a Bordeaux appellation, not part of Burgundy. Burgundy's six sub-regions, from north to south, are: Chablis, Côte de Nuits, Côte de Beaune, Côte Chalonnaise, Mâconnais, and Beaujolais.

questions.question: In Burgundy's four-tier classification system, which tier accounts for the largest share of total production?
questions.explanation: Régionale accounts for 53% of Burgundy's total production — the most basic tier and also the largest by volume.

questions.question: What does a Grand Cru label typically show?
options: Village name + vineyard name + Grand Cru
questions.explanation: A Grand Cru label is the simplest of all: it shows only the vineyard name and "Grand Cru," with no village name, because a Grand Cru is itself an independent AOC.

questions.question: What is the approximate maximum permitted yield for Premier Cru?
questions.explanation: Premier Cru's permitted yield for red wine is about 40–48 hl/ha — higher than Grand Cru (35–37) but considerably stricter than Régionale (55–60).

questions.question: If a label shows only "GEVREY-CHAMBERTIN," what tier is this?
questions.explanation: A village name shown alone, without any additional designation such as Premier Cru or Grand Cru, indicates a Village-level wine.

questions.question: What does AOC stand for?
questions.explanation: AOC stands for Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée (Controlled Designation of Origin), France's quality-assurance system for wine.

questions.question: How many Grands Crus does Burgundy have in total?
questions.explanation: Burgundy has 33 Grands Crus in total, distributed across Chablis (1), Côte de Nuits (24), and Côte de Beaune (8).

questions.question: Which word must always appear on a Premier Cru label?
questions.explanation: A Premier Cru label must always show "Premier Cru" or its abbreviation "1er Cru" to distinguish it from a Village-level wine.

questions.question: Which of the following is a Régionale-level label?
questions.explanation: Any label beginning with "Bourgogne" indicates a Régionale-level wine.

questions.question: Roughly what share of Burgundy's total production does Grand Cru account for?
questions.explanation: Grand Cru accounts for only 1% of Burgundy's total production, making it the rarest and most precious tier.

questions.question: What is the typical price range for a Village-level wine?
questions.explanation: Village-level wine typically costs €25–80, making it a good-value entry point for learning about Burgundy terroir.

questions.question: How many Grands Crus does the Côte de Nuits have?
questions.explanation: The Côte de Nuits has 24 Grands Crus, accounting for the vast majority of Burgundy's 33 total.

questions.question: Which village has the most Grands Crus (9)?
questions.explanation: Gevrey-Chambertin has 9 Grands Crus, more than any other village in the Côte de Nuits.

questions.question: What is the size of the Romanée-Conti Grand Cru?
questions.explanation: Romanée-Conti is just 1.81 hectares — one of the most expensive vineyard sites in the world.

questions.question: Which village is famous for its "feminine" style?
questions.explanation: Chambolle-Musigny is renowned for its silky texture, abundant floral aromatics, and refined, "feminine" style.

questions.question: Which is Burgundy's largest Grand Cru?
questions.explanation: Clos de Vougeot is Burgundy's largest Grand Cru, at 50.6 hectares.

questions.question: How many Grands Crus does Nuits-Saint-Georges have?
questions.explanation: Nuits-Saint-Georges has no Grand Cru, but it does have 41 Premiers Crus of exceptional quality.

questions.question: Which village is the only one in the Côte de Nuits that can produce red, white, and rosé wine?
questions.explanation: Marsannay is the only Côte de Nuits village that can produce red, white, and rosé wine.

questions.question: Which two Grands Crus does DRC (Domaine de la Romanée-Conti) hold as monopoles?
questions.explanation: DRC holds Romanée-Conti (1.81 ha) and La Tâche (6.06 ha) as exclusive monopoles.

questions.question: How many Grands Crus does Morey-Saint-Denis have?
questions.explanation: Morey-Saint-Denis has 5 Grands Crus: Clos de la Roche, Clos Saint-Denis, Clos des Lambrays, Clos de Tart, and (part of) Bonnes-Mares.

questions.question: What is the main soil type of the Côte de Nuits?
questions.explanation: The Côte de Nuits' main soil is Jurassic limestone and marl, which gives its Pinot Noir its characteristic elegance.

questions.question: How many white-wine Grands Crus does the Côte de Beaune have?
questions.explanation: The Côte de Beaune has 6 white-wine Grands Crus, all Chardonnay: Montrachet, Chevalier-Montrachet, Bâtard-Montrachet, Bienvenues-Bâtard-Montrachet, Criots-Bâtard-Montrachet, and Corton-Charlemagne.

questions.question: Which village is called the "king of white wine" yet has no Grand Cru?
questions.explanation: Meursault is the largest white-wine village in the Côte de Beaune. It has no Grand Cru, but its Premiers Crus are of exceptional quality.

questions.question: What is the size of the Montrachet Grand Cru?
questions.explanation: Montrachet is 7.5 hectares, straddling the villages of Puligny-Montrachet and Chassagne-Montrachet.

questions.question: Which village produces the Côte de Beaune's most powerful red wine?
questions.explanation: Pommard is known for its firm tannins and powerful structure — the most robust red wine of the Côte de Beaune.

questions.question: What best characterizes the style of Volnay?
questions.explanation: Volnay is known for its silky texture and abundant floral aromatics — an elegant, refined style often called "the feminine side of red wine."

questions.question: Which village, with 42 Premiers Crus, is the capital of the Côte de Beaune?
questions.explanation: Beaune is the capital of the Côte de Beaune, with 42 Premiers Crus, and its Village-level wines offer excellent value.

questions.question: What is the production breakdown of Chassagne-Montrachet?
questions.explanation: Chassagne-Montrachet produces both red and white wine in roughly equal proportions.

questions.question: What is Meursault's most famous Premier Cru?
questions.explanation: Perrières is Meursault's finest Premier Cru, closest to Grand Cru quality, with an intensely mineral character.

questions.question: How does the Côte de Beaune's main soil type differ from that of the Côte de Nuits?
questions.explanation: The Côte de Beaune's soil is mainly limestone but has a higher proportion of marl than the Côte de Nuits, which suits Chardonnay especially well.

questions.question: Which Grand Cru produces the world's most expensive Chardonnay?
questions.explanation: Montrachet produces the world's most expensive Chardonnay, averaging over €500 a bottle, with top producers reaching over €2000.

questions.question: What is Chablis's distinctive Kimmeridgian soil primarily rich in?
questions.explanation: Kimmeridgian marl is rich in tiny 150-million-year-old oyster fossils (Exogyra virgula), giving Chablis its distinctive mineral, oyster-shell character.

questions.question: How many Grands Crus does Chablis have?
questions.explanation: Strictly speaking, Chablis Grand Cru is legally a single AOC (appellation), containing 7 named Climats: Bougros, Preuses, Vaudésir, Grenouilles, Valmur, Les Clos, and Blanchot — all on the right bank of the Serein river. This differs from Gevrey-Chambertin, whose 9 Grands Crus are each their own separate AOC.

questions.question: Which is Chablis's largest and most famous Grand Cru?
questions.explanation: Les Clos is Chablis's largest Grand Cru (26.9 ha) and is widely regarded as the finest, capable of aging 30+ years.

questions.question: Which tier accounts for the largest share of production in Chablis's four-tier classification?
questions.explanation: Chablis (village level) accounts for 60% of total production — the most basic and highest-volume tier.

questions.question: What is Chablis's most classic food pairing?
questions.explanation: Chablis and oysters is a classic pairing — its minerality and marine character match beautifully, and its high acidity balances the oysters' brininess.

questions.question: What is the ideal serving temperature for Chablis?
questions.explanation: Chablis should be served at 8-10°C; too cold suppresses the aromas, though aged examples can be served slightly warmer, up to 12°C.

questions.question: Roughly how many climats (named plots) does Chablis Premier Cru have?
questions.explanation: Chablis has roughly 40 Premiers Crus, the most famous of which include Montée de Tonnerre, Fourchaume, and Vaillons.

questions.question: Which is NOT a representative producer of Chablis's traditional stainless-steel school?
questions.explanation: William Fèvre belongs to the oak-barrel (more modern) school, while Dauvissat and Raveneau represent the traditional stainless-steel school.

questions.question: What is Chablis's biggest natural threat in spring?
questions.explanation: Spring frost is Chablis's greatest threat — frosts in April-May can destroy most of a year's crop, so growers use heaters and water-spraying to protect the vines.

questions.question: La Moutonne is a monopole straddling which two Grands Crus?
questions.explanation: La Moutonne (2.35 ha) straddles Preuses and Vaudésir and is a monopole exclusively owned by Domaine Long-Depaquit.

questions.question: Which grape variety is primarily grown in Beaujolais?
questions.explanation: Beaujolais is 100% planted with Gamay — the biggest distinction from the rest of Burgundy.

questions.question: What is Beaujolais's most distinctive winemaking technique?
questions.explanation: Carbonic maceration is Beaujolais's signature winemaking technique, in which whole clusters ferment in an oxygen-free environment.

questions.question: How many Crus (special villages) does Beaujolais have?
questions.explanation: Beaujolais has 10 Crus, including Moulin-à-Vent, Morgon, and Fleurie.

questions.question: Which Cru is called the "king of Beaujolais"?
questions.explanation: Moulin-à-Vent is called the "king of Beaujolais" — the most powerful and complex, capable of aging 10-20 years, and often mistaken for Côte de Nuits Pinot Noir once aged.

questions.question: When is Beaujolais Nouveau released each year?
questions.explanation: Beaujolais Nouveau is released on the third Thursday of November each year — a French wine festival day.

questions.question: Which Cru, known for its elegant and fragrant style, is called the "queen of Beaujolais"?
questions.explanation: Fleurie is called the "queen of Beaujolais," known for violet and rose aromas and a silky texture — the most elegant and fragrant of the Crus.

questions.question: What soil type are Beaujolais's ten Crus mainly located on?
questions.explanation: The ten Crus are all on granite soils in the north — completely different from the Côte d'Or's limestone.

questions.question: What is the ideal serving temperature for Beaujolais?
questions.explanation: Beaujolais should be served lightly chilled (12-14°C), or as cool as 10°C in summer. Served at room temperature, it can taste loose and uninteresting.

questions.question: Which Cru is the only one on volcanic soil?
questions.explanation: Côte de Brouilly, on the slopes of Mont Brouilly, is the only Cru with volcanic soil, giving its wines a distinctive minerality.

questions.question: What cuisine does Beaujolais pair best with?
questions.explanation: Beaujolais's fruitiness, low tannin, and medium body make it a perfect match for Asian cuisine (Chinese, Japanese), especially dishes like kung pao chicken or sweet-and-sour pork.

questions.question: Which is the largest village in the Côte Chalonnaise?
questions.explanation: Mercurey is the largest village in the Côte Chalonnaise, focused on red wine, accounting for about 60% of the region's production.

questions.question: What is distinctive about the Bouzeron appellation?
questions.explanation: Bouzeron is the only Village-level AOC in Burgundy dedicated exclusively to Aligoté white wine.

questions.question: Which is the Mâconnais's top appellation?
questions.explanation: Pouilly-Fuissé is the Mâconnais's finest appellation, with strong minerality and good aging potential.

questions.question: Roughly how much cheaper are Côte Chalonnaise wines compared to the Côte d'Or?
questions.explanation: Côte Chalonnaise wines are about 30-50% cheaper than the Côte d'Or's, making them an excellent-value choice.

questions.question: What is distinctive about the Montagny appellation?
questions.explanation: Montagny is the only Côte Chalonnaise village dedicated exclusively to white wine, mainly Chardonnay.

questions.question: Which recent vintage is considered a "vintage of the century"?
questions.explanation: 2015 is widely recognized as a vintage of the century, with outstanding red and white wines and excellent aging potential.

questions.question: Which sub-region is Domaine de la Romanée-Conti (DRC) located in?
questions.explanation: DRC is located in Vosne-Romanée in the Côte de Nuits, holding several top-tier Grands Crus.

questions.question: Domaine Leflaive is famous for the white wines of which village?
questions.explanation: Domaine Leflaive is a top producer of Puligny-Montrachet white wine.

questions.question: Which is Chablis's benchmark producer?
questions.explanation: Domaine Raveneau is the benchmark producer for Chablis Grand Cru, known for its pure, mineral-driven style.

questions.question: What is the typical drinking window for Burgundy Grand Cru red wine?
questions.explanation: Grand Cru red wines have a solid structure and excellent aging potential, typically needing 10-30+ years to reach their peak.

questions.question: What was distinctive about the 2022 vintage?
options: Hot and dry, with outstanding whites
questions.explanation: 2022 was hot and dry, producing highly concentrated grapes, with the white wines performing especially well.

questions.question: What is the ideal temperature for a wine cellar?
questions.explanation: A steady 12-14°C is the ideal cellar temperature, allowing wine to age slowly and consistently.
